analysis.one_liner: Caps checked-baggage fees airlines charge passengers at $4.50 per bag.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and airline baggage fees remained uncapped.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred airlines from charging a checked-bag fee larger than the maximum passenger facility charge the government can levy per boarding, which is $4.50. Since carriers were routinely charging $25-$30 per checked bag at the time, this would have effectively eliminated most baggage fees. It sat in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers who check bags, and by extension any flier facing a cheaper alternative to fee-driven pricing, would pay less at the airport counter.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits an air carrier from collecting any checked-bag fee that exceeds the total passenger facility charges that could be imposed on a passenger for that flight, a maximum of $4.50 [S2][S3].
The cap would take effect 180 days after enactment, applying to both U.S. and foreign carriers flying domestic passenger routes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which collected billions of dollars a year in baggage fees during this period, would lose a major revenue stream and would likely fold some costs back into base fares.

drawbacks.text: A $4.50 cap does not reflect what it actually costs an airline to handle a bag, so carriers would likely offset lost fee revenue by raising base ticket prices, meaning travelers who never check a bag would help cover the cost for those who do [S3].
Tying the limit to passenger facility charges is an arbitrary benchmark; the fee ceiling would move with a unrelated airport charge rather than any measure of baggage-handling cost [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Checked-bag fees were a real, visible add-on cost that hit families and anyone checking luggage, and a cap would have ended that. The honest cost is pricing: airlines would have recovered revenue elsewhere, likely through higher fares spread across all passengers, so some travelers who don't check bags would pay more. The bill's simple price benchmark also ignored actual handling costs, which is a design weakness, but the core consumer benefit was straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee in July 2015, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Mica introduced the bill on July 22, 2015 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the same day, and to the Aviation Subcommittee the next day [S5].
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off: checked-bag fees, worth billions annually, stayed in place because the bill never advanced, and travelers kept paying $25-$30 per bag.

for.name: Rep. John Mica
for.role: U.S. Representative, FL-7; former chairman of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chairman, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested; the sponsor and the committee chairman were both Republicans.

industries.note: Baggage fees were a multi-billion-dollar annual revenue stream airlines carved out of the base fare after deregulation-era unbundling; the bill would have capped the fee at $4.50, ending most of that revenue. The airlines' interest in keeping the fees runs directly against travelers who check bags.
